utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to everybody. This is case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to say good afternoon on behalf of the two Judges present here today to everybody in the courtroom; the accused, the Defence teams and the Prosecution, and everybody else in this courtroom. First of all, I would like to explain why there are only two Judges sitting this afternoon. As I said last week and the week before, for professional reasons linked to the internal duties of the Judge, Judges to go back to their countries, pursuant to Rule 15 bis (A), the Judge will be absent, which allows us to continue our proceedings within the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like on behalf of the Judges absent and the two of us Judges present to extend our condolences to Mr. Coric because of his father's demise. When we were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were told by your Defence counsel that your father's health was deteriorating and all measures were taken for you to be allowed to go back to your country, and that was done last week. So I would like to express the Chamber's condolences, and I'm sure that everybody else joins me in expressing our sympathies for you for having lost a father. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I'd like to thank you for allowing me to attend my father's funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have a new witness. The witness is present. But before we have the witness shown in, I'd like to give you some information, and I would like to turn to the Prosecution with respect to (redacted), who is to come in due course. I think that Counsel Kovacic wants to say something. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Kovacic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like to make an oral submission, and I think it is linked to the situation that we find ourselves in at present. This is it: I consider that the Prosecution, over the past week, linked to bringing in (redacted), (redacted), is proceeding in a manner which makes it impossible for the Defence to prepare themselves to cross-examine the witness and to prepare for the witness in general. And it is in that sense that I'd like to suggest that the Trial Chamber issue instructions and guidelines to the Prosecution in order to ensure a just and fair trial, and that is that the Trial Chamber should make rulings in order to ensure a fair trial. This is the matter in hand. The first point I'd like to raise is this: The Prosecutor is providing the wrong information to the Defence teams, and of course to the Trial Chamber in the same way, with respect to the scope of the expected testimony of that witness. Specifically speaking, this is how things stand: You know full well, because you received the same documents from the Prosecution that we do, that with every witness we are able to extract from the viva voce witness list, to extract the portion which relates to the witness in question, and several days after that, usually before the witness is brought in, the Prosecutor supplies us with what is known as the proofing chart, which is a more detailed list in which they state the documents that they're going to use with the witness during that witness's testimony, and also they provide us to references of paragraphs in the indictment and the counts in the indictment as well. And that proofing chart should, in fact, be a list which you, Your Honours, pursuant to your order of the 30th of November, 2005, asked for. However, it still does not contain all the elements. Now, one the differences between those two lists or charts is the following: In the first viva voce witness list, we are provided with a summary of that witness's testimony, and there is a column in which the paragraphs and counts are listed, and the names of the accused are stated to whom those paragraphs or counts relate, at least as far as -- what the Prosecution considers to be relevant. Now, this other material in the proofing chart, as a rule a series of paragraphs and counts in the indictment are added without mentioning the names of the accused specifically. However, the names of the accused to which testimony relates is something that can be found out if you look at the numbers of the paragraphs of the indictment, the numbers listed, because in the proofing chart, you'll see that it relates to paragraph 7 and 8 of the indictment, then it is quite obviously my client because he is the accused related to those paragraphs. Now, what happened in this case, in the case of the documents which refer to (redacted), that during the -- in the viva voce list, that is to say the first listing, the Prosecution states that that particular witness will speak about Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic. Now, in the proofing chart, when you take it paragraph by paragraph in order, you will find that that particular witness, with respect to the paragraphs, also this refers to the accused Prlic, then later on you come across the accused Coric, and a little further down you will come across the accused Pusic, and then you come to paragraphs which relate to all the accused, paragraphs in which all the accused are named, either where the legal arguments come in or at the end of the whole -- all the paragraphs. So I think that this procedure is contrary to your ruling - that's my first point - because it makes it impossible for us to see where they're going because we have a contradiction between the two papers, between the two documents, which is contrary to your ruling and tends to cloud the issue generally, because the Defence, when it examines the list, finds it difficult to assess which facts relate to which accused and so on and so forth, and how this will be linked to the evidence and the exhibits. So the first argument is that the Prosecution is providing the wrong information to the Defence and, by the same token, to the Trial Chamber with respect to the scope and subject of the testimony, which affects our preparation. Now, the second point is this: Along with that, the Prosecution, much too late, discloses documents linked to the witness, and especially is running late with the translations into the language which the accused can understand. And when they hand out the material - and when I say "material" I mean the 66 -- Rule 66 material and Rule 68 material disclosure - and in order to save time I'm not going to interpret things here or present separate arguments and say that documents pursuant to Rule 66 should have been disclosed far earlier on, and I would like to say that usually we get them just before the witness appears. So a lot of those documents were not disclosed on time, but I don't want to dwell on that for the moment. So in respect of this witness, the Prosecutor first of all sent in extensive material to the Defence which related to the witness, which is predominantly -- which was predominantly in Spanish. I do not consider that to be disclosed to us, because Defence counsel are not duty-bound to know Spanish. They are duty-bound to know English or French, and of course they know their own language, B/C/S, but it is not a requirement for them to speak Spanish. Now, on the 14th of June, the Prosecution, in the EDS system, disclosed another portion of the material, and we don't know, nor were we told whether that material relates to that particular witness alone or whether it also includes that witness. After that, the Prosecution -- and let me say that we contacted during the weekend -- the Prosecution during the weekend or, rather, on Friday and Saturday, I sent them two letters myself. The Prosecution on Friday evening, so on the 16th of June, that is, at 1800 hours, when people are not in their offices any longer, sent a fax with an index and an attending letter and said that the package contains 40 new documents, an addition of 40 new documents, which were not stipulated in the proofing chart, and the list's there. And let me also say that that listing was not a complete one because it begins with page 8. Now, the next morning, that is to say on Saturday morning, the 17th of June, we were able to pick the material up in our pigeonholes, the material provided by fax to us, and that's what we did. We fetched the material. And I must say that the Prosecution was very obliging, because it put it all on CD, on compact disk, and we were provided with two copies of the CD so that we could provide our clients with one of those CDs since the CD has a lot of the texts already translated into B/C/S. Although I'm very grateful for that gesture, for providing me with a compact disk on Saturday morning, I must say that I need four and a half minutes for copying the CD, so thank you for saving those four and half minutes of my time, but let me say that we need a lot of days and many staff to check the list against the charts. So it was only on Saturday that we were provided with the documents, including the translations into B/C/S, but unfortunately, up until this point in time, according to my information, we are still lacking 160 translations into the language which the accused understand, give or take two or three documents, but roughly speaking approximately 160, because it's become a forest, very dense forest, and you can't count all the trees. Anyway, I think that this is very irrelevant, because we still do not have all the translations available. Pursuant to the rules of the detention centre, the Defence is not able to provide the accused with the material and documents before Monday morning because we don't have access during the weekend unless we are -- make a request of the Trial Chamber to allow us to do this if we have received the documents during the previous week, which means that in actual fact the accused cannot be given the material and documents for this week. Specifically this relates to Wednesday of this week. And you should also bear in mind the fact that the material and documents which, according to the Prosecutor's allegations, we were given connected to (redacted)is four thick binders, and they total 281 documents, and they are mostly very long, extensive documents on many pages. Of those 281 documents, as I say, 160 of them, approximately, have still not been translated. So I don't have to explain to you that we cannot look at those documents nor can the accused look through those documents in the space of two days and give me instructions, whereas the accused were there, of course, I was not. Nor can the Defence teams with all the teams and staff working with them can do this. And I want to be benevolent to the Prosecution and say that I can't even leaf through 160 documents let alone anything else. So as I say, the Defence did contact the Prosecution. We told them of the situation. We communicated by phone, but we weren't able to convince them of anything or prevail upon them in any way. I think that, based on these events, this makes it impossible for the Defence to work normally, particularly because we need reasonable time to go through such a large number of documents and prepare for the examination. And I think you are quite aware that the burden of proof is on the Prosecution. They are the active part. The Prosecution has to decide when they're going to bring in what witness. So it is up to them to see whether they have the material that they need to disclose and provide the Defence with, whether they have all the translations of the material, and whether they have indeed disclosed the material to the Defence in a reasonable scope of time. If those conditions are not met, they cannot go ahead with their witnesses, because this is a constant race and we're always lagging behind because the Prosecution doesn't seem to be able to see if they have everything they need to have and to coordinate that with the timetable and scheduling of the witnesses. Of course I'm not even going to mention the Defence's work on the weekend, Saturday and Sunday, and I mean all the Defence teams, all the Defence counsel and the staff, because that's become -- become quite usual and customary. I myself am personally ready to give up my weekends but I must say that it's difficult to make my whole team do so. We have to work every Saturday and every Sunday, and that has gone beyond all limits. But even if we leave that point behind, I would like to focus on my main points. And let me also just mention one matter. Your Honours, perhaps you feel that we are exaggerating. You also know that there is a schedule and a timetable and that we have to have -- proceed at a certain rate, and I think we're lagging behind already. And now the Defence, to make up for that lagging behind, they want to make it up at the debit of the Defence. And as you know, the Defence teams have limited resources and limited personnel, and we have no possibility of increasing our resources because the limits are set by the Registrar. So I would like to propose that (redacted) planned for this week be deferred, be postponed. Second, that the Trial Chamber should indicate to the Prosecution that the materials they plan to use along with any witness, including (redacted), must be disclosed at least three weeks before these people testify, in the official languages of the Court and the languages understood by the accused, pursuant to Rule 66 and Rule 68. And thirdly, that the proofing chart should be prepared in such a way as was required and demanded by the Trial Chamber in its ruling or to find a compromise solution to improve transparency because there is no transparency for the time being. You cannot say that that witness is going to address matters referring to the Accused X and then you see that it wasn't this X, it was Mr. Y or whatever. So that method has to be improved in the interests of transparency, and it must become quite clear, explicitly stated to which accused the documents refer. So those are my proposals, Your Honour. I'm of course at the Court's disposal for any additional explanation that you would like to have from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Counsel Karnavas, just a few minutes, please. I think everything's already been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to be a little more concrete to some extent. What this entailed was this: Us getting the material approximately 7.00 on Friday afternoon. Our staff would look at it on Saturday. I had two staff members working Saturday and Sunday full time just to put the material in binders and collate it and organise it, realising that there's also 40 additional documents. Now, you might say, well, (redacted)is not going to be here until Wednesday, but we're preparing for Monday and Tuesday, and it's impossible to be in court doing your job and at the same time knowing that you've got four binders to go through. In this particular case, we have at least one accused, and that is Mr. Praljak, who has specifically indicated that he wishes to actively participate in his own Defence, but each and every one of the accused is entitled to assist in their own Defence and one way of assisting is to go through the documents and have them in a language which they can understand and appreciate. Now, just to highlight one point Mr. Kovacic made. The Prosecution chooses when they're going to bring in these witnesses. There are lots of witnesses that are not documentary witnesses, a lot of witnesses they can bring in that don't cause a dilemma. When they do these things, it really stresses the Defence to its absolute limits, and it -- and this is becoming a trial by attrition. There is only so much that we can do. We have a limited budget, but it's exhausting, and this is not a fair process. Lastly, what I want to point out is an observation that I over the weekend, thinking about what happened last week with Mr. Beese. It took approximately 45 minutes, at the most, to introduce all of the documents that Mr. Beese -- through Mr. Beese that the Prosecution wished, documents generated by the -- the European observers. Now, based on what you've already told us, Mr. President - and I totally agree with you - is that when a document comes in, that entire document in its totality is fair game, any part of it. But think about it: Mr. Mundis said that if he were to spend one minute on each document, it would take approximately six hours. When you have all those documents being introduced within a matter of 10 or 15 minutes, and then if we go back to our approach of our time, the Defence time, should be equal to the Prosecution's time, you can see where the problem lies. And we're going to have a problem with all of these documents because we're responsible to go through all of them at one point or at some point. I think the Trial Chamber may wish to reconsider or at least think about the possibility of first requesting from the Prosecution that they make some sort of a demonstrable effort to tell us, to show us why a particular document is relevant, rather than asking the witness, "Is this relevant to the period at hand?" I think the onus is on the Prosecution, or on the moving party, to show why a document has some indicia or relevancy to this particular case. At least that might narrow the number of documents. But I think we need to know concretely why a particular document is being introduced by the Prosecution. I think that's only fair when they're bringing in all these documents. I just throw that out. I ask you to consider it, and I'm sure you will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Counsel Karnavas. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution for the response, just a few observations on my part. If my colleague Judge Trechsel wishes to intervene, he will do so, but as far as I'm concerned this is what I would like to say, and I'm just speaking in my own name. I was aware of the problems that you have raised, and I have been aware of them since November, because I know that those kinds of problems will inevitably arise, first of all because there are a lot of documents in this trial, and secondly because I thought that -- I was sure that the documents wouldn't be all translated on time in the language of the accused. So for that reason, I did ask in November -- I asked the Prosecution to provide me with the chart, the proofing chart, the chart with witnesses, the exhibits, the paragraphs -- relevant paragraphs of the indictment, and all the other indications with respect to responsibility and accountability of 7(1) and 7(3) of the accused. Now, as you know, that request of mine was not complied with integrally. Unfortunately, we saw that the Prosecution wasn't able to comply with the November ruling, or not entirely with the November ruling. Now, with that in mind, the Prosecution did tell us that in September they would provide us with that famous chart, which would be a response to the ruling made by the Chamber and so that we could have this by the beginning of September, that we could have a comprehensive and integral vision of everything that is going to happen in the future. But from this time onwards until September, especially for the witnesses coming in in June and July, the Prosecution will also have to provide for those witnesses a list of witnesses and exhibits. I listened to what you said very carefully. I listened to the explanations, and I think you said that on -- you said on Friday, around about 7.00, that the Prosecution sent you information, faxed you information, or e-mailed you information of the material that they were going to provide you with, and then you found out that among all those documents there were actually 281 documents, you said, and among those 281, 160 had not yet been translated into B/C/S. You also just told me that you had to work on Saturday morning, and that because of the rules governing the Detention Centre you were not able to contact your clients, so that the accused only had knowledge of those documents as of today. I'd like to tell you that I am highly aware of the difficulties that the Defence in general encounters, and that is why I as the Judge would like to say that the Defence must be given the necessary time to meet with the accused and to be able to discuss with the accused the documents. Now, if they are unable to meet with the accused and discuss these problems on a weekend, then I don't see what we're going to do and how the Defence counsel will be able to meet with their clients. Now, a few months ago I said that in view of the nature of these proceedings where we have a record number of exhibits, it seemed to me to be important, both for the Defence and for the Prosecution and for the Judges, that the Defence be able to have the necessary time accorded them to be able to do their work and also to have enough time to meet with the accused. For that reason, I suggested that you should have the freedom on a Friday, that you should be able, on a Friday and on Monday morning, to have meetings, that is to say to have meetings with your clients on Monday afternoon and to be able to prepare for the cross-examination. When you have a case with several hundred documents, of course this can be done very quickly, but in this particular trial and with (redacted), which you have 281 different documents, and certain trials have introduced as many documents in a short space of time as were introduced during a whole trial. So I'd like to tell you that I'm very aware of the problems in hand, and in our ruling of November I wanted you to have an overall view of the Prosecution's intentions, and I take note, together with you today, that you are encountering difficulties. Having said that, we have to ensure a -- a speedy trial. That does not only mean expeditious. A speedy trial means that we must respect all the facets of a proper trial, a just trial. And when you have tens of thousands of documents, then those documents have to be studied, and the questions raised in those documents must be pertinent and useful to the Judges. So I understand fully that the Defence teams have many questions to raise with respect to documents, and those were voiced by Mr. Karnavas as well. So those are the problems that we're all faced with, all of us together, and I personally think that, at the very least, the Prosecution should provide the Defence a fortnight before they bring in a witness all the documents listed which will be used. And, of course, those documents have to be translated because, as you have already indicated, you are there to help the accused, to assist them, but you have to work together because the accused give their own observations on the documents and thereby build up a defence strategy. And as you very rightly underlined, there are certain accused who want to ask the questions themselves. So the accused must have the documents provided in their own language. Of course, if you don't know Spanish, how can you be expected to interpret documents that are in Spanish? These quite impossible. So we're faced with a very real problem here. Now, you're asking that we postpone the (redacted) (redacted). There are two ways of proceeding: Either to postpone it for a period of time or go ahead with the examination-in-chief and postpone the cross-examination. But having listened to you, another idea -- I have got another idea, and I don't understand why we can't bring in witnesses where there are no problems with the documents and the translations, and bring in the international witnesses later on, at a later stage. Why not bring in fact witnesses first where we don't have this problem of documents and language, and then leave the important international witnesses, ambassadors and other internationals, until a later stage? Well, we have so far had a mixture. We had internationals, we had fact witnesses, and so on, and of course this has led to problems. Without further ado, the Prosecution can go ahead, unless my colleague Judge Trechsel wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would first of all like to hear the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Ibrisimovic. I'm going to give you the floor and then the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I see another problem here which could crop up, and that is the introduction of new documents. We started with a list of 9.490 documents, which was provided. We have 9.607, which means more than 100 new documents within the space of a month. The Defence made no objection, but I fear that there must -- might be a hyperproduction of documents, and that this figure of approximately 10.000 will be overstepped. So it is my proposal that we have a meeting scheduled in future to see how we can get round this issue and help us -- help all the parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, there won't be 10.000 documents, but several thousand additional documents, perhaps, which is a real problem. I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution now. May we hear their sentiments on the different problems that were raised, and let me say that we've already spent almost an hour discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours Mr. President and Judge Trechsel. In connection with -- well, let me say many things have been said in the last 45 minutes. I will try to touch upon those that seem to me the most basic, and of course if I miss something, I'm sure the Chamber will correct me. In terms of the general observation -- some of the general observations made by counsel, I must say the Prosecution takes exception to that in -- for the most part. I suppose it's a bit of the old saying whether the glass is half empty or half full. The Prosecution has for many months now engaged in very, very extended and substantial efforts dealing with a large -- undoubtedly a large volume of complex material, and for the most part I think the disclosure and the preparation has gone, if I may say so, I think for the most part rather well. So we do not accept any broad allegations or criticisms of any wide-scale problems in this respect. I say this in this context as well, in terms of the frequent references to the number of -- the size of the Prosecution team. I can assure Your Honours as I stand here this afternoon that if you look around the courtroom and, including the lawyers of the Prosecution that are outside this courtroom, there are substantially more lawyers and case managers and paralegals working for the Defence than there are for the Prosecution. And if anyone disputes that, I will be happy to put our rosters side by side. It is simply not true. Our team is working extremely hard. Our teams work on the weekend as well, almost all weekends, as I did myself this weekend. Indeed, everyone, I'm sure, on both sides -- all sides, are working very hard. Again, I take exception to the allegation that there is substantial discrepancies between the Rule 65 ter summaries and the proofing charts. Yes, indeed, as we have said repeatedly, when a witness comes to The Hague, some of whom have not been seen for a substantial period of time, provide some additional information or clarification, that has to be reflected and often leads to some supplemental disclosure, but by and large, Your Honour, we do not accept that there are any substantial contradictions or discrepancies between the original summaries and those that are provided on a more recent basis. Don't -- don't -- do not accept that. In terms of the allegations that has been made about the -- which witness goes to each accused, again I think there is a misunderstanding and I think that's being used or mischaracterised in the nature of the evidence. As we said in our 65 ter witness list filing on the 19th of January, 2006 - I'm referring to page 2 of our filing, paragraph number 5 - "Except as expressly indicated in paragraph 230 of the amended indictment, all of the evidence is against all of the accused. Using the illustration of a more usual case involving only one accused, all the Prosecution is against that accused. There is no one else or nothing else against which some other part of the evidence is used. All of the Prosecution evidence is against all of the accused except where we have specifically stated to the contrary. All the crime base evidence goes to all of the accused. All the common jurisdictional element evidence goes to all of the accused." So we did not in our charts and do not now list for each item of evidence all six names every time, because that would be entirely repetitive and redundant, for every piece of evidence to put all six names. We have in some instances where a particular document or a particular witness substantially talks about a particular accused by name, and we know that by reading the statement, then we have indeed put that -- endeavoured to put that in all of our summary material or our disclosure material, but by and large, if there is any effort by the Defence to make some broad distinction that this goes to this accused, this goes to this accused, this goes to this accused, that is a misunderstanding of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. The vast majority of the Prosecution evidence goes to every accused because we have to establish the crime base for the counts of the indictment that go to each of the accused. Again, where there is something that is very specific as to a particular accused, we have endeavoured to highlight that. So again, we reject -- with all respect to Mr. Kovacic, I do not accept the broad criticisms that he has made toward the Prosecution in this respect. Now, in connection with the Spanish Battalion materials, Your Honour, I just want to look at my notes and make sure that we shouldn't be in private session. I don't think we need be for this purpose. There has indeed been some difficulty with this particular set of materials because of -- they not only have to be translated, first of all, into English, or at least one of the official languages of the Tribunal, which in this case, for better or worse, happens to be English, and secondly, they have then to be translated into Spanish. So this represented a situation -- excuse me, B/C/S. My apology. This represents an absolute doubling of the work involved, and the Tribunal does not even employ, regularly employ Spanish translation staff. All this material has been had to be sent outside the institution to contract translators to have these translations made. Now, I will be the first to say that I was under the impression until late last week that we were further along than we were, and I have to say that in all transparency to the Court. I thought that more of the B/C/S translations had been completed as of the end of last week. My most current information is that of the approximately 260, or someone says 280, Spanish Battalion documents, a little less than half have -- are presently in B/C/S. That's my understanding. So indeed there are a number of B/C/S translations that remain outstanding. As to the English translations, an the official language of the Tribunal, most of those have been available -- Your Honour, it is our position that most of those have been available for some time. Now, I would say, Your Honour, this: As to the Spanish Battalion documents, I think -- and for the witness, I think we should proceed and do the best we can. We don't know how we're -- the week may take us. There are additional days before the witness is called. A lot of these documents, like many of these reporting documents, just as the Chamber will have seen with some of the ECMM documents, often it is only a particular paragraph of a three- or four- or ten-page document that is relevant to the case. One need not review the entire document because there may be something in that report about something that happened in Tuzla or somewhere else, or in Zagreb or in Belgrade, and the pertinent parts of the material can often be identified in a much more limited way. Now, having said that, I'm not dismissing -- let my say again I'm not dismissing the volume of the work involved for the Defence as with the Prosecution as well. I'm just suggesting that we go forward, we call -- (redacted)is here in The Hague, we present -- we take his testimony and we conduct at least his direct examination and see where the week takes us. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I will summarise briefly what you have just stated. You acknowledge that generally, speaking, the Defence has reason to point to certain problems, although not overall. With regard to translations from Spanish into B/C/S, you say that the services of those not employed at the Tribunal had to be used. This is not your responsibility, but that is why some documents have not been translated. You also pointed to the fact that the Spanish documents are quite voluminous but that certain passages would be useful and relevant for this case. You also say that with reference to events in Tuzla or Zagreb, these do not relate to the testimony or, rather, the examination of this witness. Furthermore, you say that you see no obstacle to postpone the cross-examination of this witness when the Defence has all the documents at their disposal. I have taken note of and listened carefully to what you have said. You have in fact not replied to any of the questions I put to you. For example, why you don't bring in witnesses with whom there would be no problem with regard to documents, leaving international witnesses until the end of the trial. But of course it is up to you to decide how to proceed and you leave open to the Judges the possibility of Draconian measures. However, so far this International Tribunal has not issued too many directives either to the Prosecution or to the Defence, leaving it up to you to decide how to proceed. This witness could be brought in and the cross-examination delayed. I don't know whether Judge Trechsel has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... nevertheless, I wonder whether a broad discussion of general questions is conducive to the speedy and rapid and smooth continuation of the -- of the proceedings. I think the Prosecution will be aware of the fact that the preparation of the hearing of (redacted)did not run the way it has, and I'm confident they will learn the lesson. I think for the moment the best thing is to go ahead with interrogation this week, have the main, and then probably for cross we will have to postpone that. I absolutely accept that the Defence is right, and I think we could start with the witness for today now. That would be my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave. Since I have raised this issue, I cannot refrain from saying some things. Of course, one of the possible solutions, which would go a long way toward rectifying this imbalance and incorrect way of proceeding, is to separate the cross-examination from the examination-in-chief. I would, however, ask the Chamber, before issuing a definite decision about this, to consider the following: The Defence can, of course, live with this, but there are two problems. One, the Chamber hears a witness, and the testimony consists of two parts, examination-in-chief and cross. This gives the Chamber an impression of the testimony of that witness, an impression of matters pertaining to weight, and so on and so forth. This Tribunal and every court recognises the principle that both -- it would be best that both parts were heard as a whole. Of course, there will be cases when we will not be able to do that. However, when such major and important witnesses are called, this should be avoided. That's why I ask that when we have received all the translations and prepared, we bring this witness in and hear the entirety of his testimony. That's the first point I wish to raise. Secondly, I will not respond to everything stated by the Prosecutor, but I do wish to touch upon the following: I cannot agree with what the Prosecutor says when he mentions the human resources available to both sides. The Prosecutor says when we take into account the whole team that we see in the courtroom today plus those in the office, there are fewer of them than there are of us on the Defence side. But my client is one of six accused. He could be tried on his own or together with 16 others. But I as his Defence counsel am up against the OTP. Each one of us is conducting his own defence, and according to the rules of our profession and the rules of these proceedings, each one of is duty-bound to conduct his own defence. Of course, we try to cooperate whenever this is possible. But, Your Honours, the next witness and the witnesses we are discussing now, I have to say that for these witnesses each Defence team has prepared as if they were doing this on their own. And another thing I have to say for the record, Your Honours: The Prosecutor has given the Defence some good advice. He said you needn't look into all the documents. Your Honours, I think I would lose my licence to practice law if I were to behave like this, because if I could find a single word or a line or a passage that makes this document relevant, of course I have to read all this in order to find that word or that line. Once I find it, I go further in my analysis. Your Honours, you yourselves have imposed this as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What you are saying is relevant and interesting and understandable, but it's not really necessary to go broadly into every argument of the other side just to keep your head up and swimming maybe arm's length further down the stream. I wonder whether it's necessary and I invite you to limit yourself to what we really have to hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept your criticism. I just wish to point to two major examples. I ask Your Honours to consider once again, because this is becoming the pattern now. We also have Witness Beese. Is it in line with the most important principles here to separate the direct and the cross? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I support my colleague Mr. Kovacic fully, and with respect to what we have said so far, I have something to add very briefly. Today, the OTP has confirmed that in the documents handed over to us there are parts not directly linked to our indictment. If we look at the documents carefully, we will see that there are entire documents which are not linked either to the territory or the time frame of the indictment, and there are some documents which do not refer at all to the events described in our indictment. The central issue to be discussed today is who is to select the relevant documents which are tendered into evidence by the Prosecution? It is my impression that the OTP wishes to simply shift all the documents at their disposal relating to certain geographical areas, regardless of the places and times mentioned in the indictment, to the Court and the Defence, asking them to make a selection and find the relevant documents. I feel that this practice is impermissible and that the Prosecution should be obliged to state precisely for each and every document to which paragraph in the indictment it refers. I feel that in this way the OTP will stop disclosing hundreds of documents and will make it easier for all of us to conduct these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall soon issue a written decision in connection with the admissibility of documents. So we will respond to this question. In the meantime, we have to proceed. Even if delaying the cross-examination is not an ideal solution, the Judges do pay special attention to the fact that the testimony of a witness should be evaluated as a whole based on both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, and we shall do everything in our power to avoid any prejudice to you. The fact that the witness will return for the cross-examination will give you ample time to prepare, and in this way your cross-examination will certainly be more productive than it would be were it to take place immediately after the examination-in-chief. Because of all the problems that have arisen with translations of documents, we shall postpone the cross-examination for (redacted) until a later date, and the Judges feel unanimously that this is the best solution. Should there be any scheduling problems, of course all this has to be taken into account in order to ensure a fair trial. We have now spent a whole hour on these issues, but of course these issues had to be raised. Before I ask the usher to fetch the witness for today, there is one further point I wish to clarify. Next week, on the 29th of June, Thursday, there will be a Plenary Session for all the Judges. This is an important Plenary Session, and for this reason it would be a good idea for the witness planned for next week to be here on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, to be examined on those three days, and we might have to leave a witness for later. Mr. Mundis -- Mr. Scott, do we agree? Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please fetch the witness. We have about 25 minutes left before the break. OTP you have the floor. I said 25 minutes before the break, not 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I will keep that in mind. Before the witness enters, maybe I'll just inform the Trial Chamber the relevant paragraphs and counts that will be related to this witness. It will be paragraphs 63, 64, 66 and 67, and the relevant counts will be count 1, count 2, count 3, count 8, count 9, count 15, count 16, count 17, count 19, count 20, and count 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bos. Thank you for what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'd just like to see if you can hear me in a language you can understand. I'll be listening to you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that you're speaking English. So you've understood what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first name is Jacqueline, my surname is Carter, and my date of birth is 8th of May, 1962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me, madam, what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My current profession, I'm a military general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, and 1994, what was your function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same. I was still serving in the army as a general practitioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have you ever testified before a court, an international or national court of law about the events in Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you now read the solemn declaration handed to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Madam, just a few explanations from me before I give the floor to Mr. Bos. You were cited as a Prosecution witness by the Prosecution. You're going to start off by answering questions put to you by the representative of the OTP - you already know him - and once he completes his examination, the Defence counsel sitting to your left, who represent the people sitting at the back, are going to ask you their questions within the scope of cross-examination, and you'll see that there is a difference in the way in which this is conducted. There is a difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination, where your answers will be yes or no. Now, there are two Judges sitting this afternoon, and we might be asking you some questions as well. You have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, which excludes any mendacity, so please try and answer the questions as best as possible. If you have any difficulties, please let us know. So before the next technical break, we still have a quarter of an hour, so we'll go on for 15 minutes, have a break, and then continue. Mr. Bos, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Carter. You told the Trial Chamber that you were a military general practitioner. When did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I joined the army in February, 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us your career in the army as of 1989.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I served my first two years as regimental medical officer in Bielefeld, in Germany, and then moved to British military hospital Iserlohn, also in Germany, to do an obstetrics and gynecology job, so completing my general practice training. In February, 1992, I returned to United Kingdom to serve in Tidworth, which is a military base in the south of England, as a qualified general practitioner and a regimental medical officer to the 1st Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Fusiliers. While serving in Tidworth, I was informed that I was to move from that post as and when the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Battle Group deployed to former Yugoslavia as part of the UN force. I joined that battle group in October, 1992, and served with them for a six-month tour of duty. I then returned to the United Kingdom and continued to serve as a military general practitioner in a variety of bases throughout UK, during which time I did two further tours of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. I spent four years as a senior medical officer in Cyprus, returning to UK in 2002 to assume a non-clinical post of regional clinical director for army primary health care services based in the West Midlands; and since May, 2005, I have been the senior medical officer in army training Regiment Pirbright.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Carter. You just stated that -- that you had two further tours in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you tell us during which periods you were there again and where you were.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: My second tour was in the handover from United Nations to NATO forces from January to June, July, 1996, when I was based in Vitez, and my third tour was in March to September, 1998, when I was based in Sipovo, but in that tour I had the responsibility of being the senior medical officer, and as such was responsible for the whole of the delivery of the general practice service by British forces, so travelled through -- throughout the British area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to focus your attention now on the period the first time you were in the former Yugoslavia, which was from October to April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you said that you were a medical officer attached to the 1 Cheshire Battle Group.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. And was this an UNPROFOR group?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was an UNPROFOR group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this unit also been referred to as BritBat?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell us under which chain of command you operated in that unit?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The medical detachment that I was working with, our direct chain of command was back to the National Support Element based in Tomislavgrad. However, on a day-to-day basis, I worked for officer commanding Bravo Company for 1 Cheshire Battle Group based in Gornji Vakuf, and indirectly therefore on day-to-day basis also for Lieutenant Colonel Bob Stewart, the commanding officer of 1 Cheshire Battle Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: At the time I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what -- what your job description was.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I was responsible for the delivery of role one medical care for the UNPROFOR troops based in Gornji Vakuf, other UNPROFOR troops who were passing through our area of responsibility, and other specific aid agencies for -- or NGOs, for example, UNHCR. By role one medical facility, by role one medical care, I mean immediate lifesaving medical treatment, stabilisation of casualties for extraction to a hospital facility, and the delivery of day-to-day general practice family type medicine, coughs and colds, and also providing and occupational health facility, for example considering the effect of the environment in which we were living, the factory and the dust and how that might be affecting the soldiers' health.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how large was the medical team you worked with?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: There was myself as the doctor, I had one medical sergeant, and approximately ten junior soldiers which were a mixture of medics and drivers. And during the period of the conflict, the fighting period, I also had attached a small number of bandsmen from the 1 Cheshire's Battalion themselves, because in the British army bandsmen are also trained as a second trade as medics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what vehicles did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We had three kinds of vehicles. We had normal Land Rovers, we had wheeled ambulances, and we had armoured ambulances, which I colloquially refer to as 432s. Those vehicles are very old and do not have the advantage of the armoured protection that you might associate with armoured vehicles. For example, they don't have the chobham that is on the side of a Warrior, but they are tracked vehicles and therefore look like a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just -- just to get back to your -- to a question that I asked you earlier. You've been referring to "bandsmen" and maybe some of the people here in the court don't know what bandsmen are. Could you explain what bandsmen are.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: In 1992, the British army had a very large number of military bands, and each battalion more or less had a military band where the musicians are also soldiers, and so those soldiers -- there isn't much of a military role for playing a clarinet or a big bass drum, so they are secondarily trained as medics and are sometimes used as stretcher bearers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In what kind of building was the BritBat company regiment housed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We were housed in what had been a -- a small factory complex which was used for a light engineering company, the exact details of which I'm not aware. There was still evidence of some of the machinery still in the building, but on the whole the building was more or less empty at the time that we were using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you involved in the early inspection before the regiment actually moved into this building?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: As is traditional with British army deployments, the medical units deploy early in order to have integrated medical support on the ground for the incoming troops, and as such, once the site had been selected, that the factory had been selected as the site for our base in Gornji Vakuf, I moved up-country with the other command element of B Company ahead of the other troops that were going to occupy the building, and as such was one of the first -- I think there were about 20 of us who were first resident in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you inspected that building, did you -- did you discover any particular -- any particularity?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: There were two areas of the building complex that caused concern. One was in a small outbuilding where there was bloodstaining and what appeared to be evidence of cerebrospinal fluid marking the walls and extensive bloodstaining on the floor of that building. The bloodstaining and cerebrospinal fluid was at a height of about five and a half to six feet, so considerably a little bit taller than myself, and was associated with evidence of what appeared to be human hair. The second area was in what was the plant room for the boilers of this building, where there appeared to be ropes, chains, and other associated paraphernalia that were left in a -- in positions that led one to postulate that that could well have been used as a site for torture, including hanging insofar as that the ropes were hung over high structures with nooses held -- with noose-like configuration of the ropes hanging beneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've been referring to feet, and maybe some of us in court are not familiar with feet. Would you be able to tell us -- you're saying around six feet. Would you be able to say how that would be in metres?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Approximately 1 metre 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Apologies for my Englishness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know which -- do you know who had previously occupied the factory?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I was led to believe that the building had previously been occupied by the HVO, and to that end I understood that a gentleman who I recollect was called Avdo had been the HVO's representative left to oversee our use of that building, and he remained working alongside us during certainly the six months that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you confront this Mr. Avdo with your findings?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We did. On inspecting the building and finding the two aforementioned areas, it was raised with Mr. Avdo as to our concerns as to what had gone on and as to whether in fact it was likely that this was -- particularly that this was blood and cerebrospinal fluid from a health and safety perspective if nothing else. He was not prepared to answer our questions and was quite dismissive and a little cagey about his responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may put in a question. How do you recognise blood? That we more or less can imagine, but what about spinal fluid? How did you know this was spinal fluid? Did you analyse the traces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a very classic association between when blood and cerebrospinal fluid are exuded from the body. There is a very typical pattern of the way in which the blood and cerebrospinal fluid separate and leave their two separate traces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you perhaps explain what you mean by spinal fluid. I must confess that I'm not quite familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It is the fluid that surrounds the brain. It's the fluid that surrounds the brain and down the spinal cord. So seeing cerebrospinal fluid implies that there has been significant brain injury, with exposure of underlying tissues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now a medical precision: The liquid, if it is red, what -- if blood is red, what is the cerebrospinal fluid's colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very, very pale yellowy -- straw-type coloured, very pale, but not as clear as water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe now is a good time for a break, Your Honours. I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is a quarter to four. We reconvene at approximately 4.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, before we continue, I just want to clarify one thing and I apologise for not doing that at the start. What is your current rank --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. No microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I don't know if -- I'll repeat the question, but -- so my question was what is your current rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I currently have acting rank, which means I am wearing the rank of full colonel, but in fact I'm still actually a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And for this examination would you prefer I refer you to as "Lieutenant Colonel" or "Doctor"? What is your preference?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I have no preference. It really doesn't -- I'm used to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll refer to you then as Lieutenant Colonel Carter. Lieutenant Colonel Carter, when the units moved into this base, this was the B Company of the Cheshire group. Now, how many soldiers are contained in a company?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Normally a company is the strength of about 120 soldiers and officers, but when deployed on ops - operations - that figure rises to more like 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And so were there 150 soldiers in the base in total or were there any other units also occupying the base?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: In addition to B Company of 1st Battalion Cheshire Regiment, there were also seven armoured workshops who are also of about -- strength of about 120; and in addition, there were elements of an engineers support unit as well as ourselves. We're not -- as a medical attachment, we were also not included in the original figures of the Cheshire's Battle Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So how many soldiers or persons would be in the base in total?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Approximately 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who was -- what was the name of the commander of the -- of the B Company?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: For the first part of the tour B Company was commanded by Major Alistair Rule, 1 Cheshire, and towards the middle of January his tour of duty was finished and he was replaced by Major Alun Jones, 1 Royal Irish Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What were your daily activities in the first two months of your duty?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: My primary duty, as I previously stated, was to provide medical care to the soldiers in the camp. We ran a sick parade in the morning usually, and another one in the evening, but were available to see soldiers during the day and out of those hours if required. In addition to that, part of my remit was, in order to understand the lay of the area of responsibility that we were to look after, in other words, the Gornji Vakuf opstina predominantly, and to understand the medical capability and the medical facilities that were available on the ground to military and civilian personnel, and to have an idea of the populations that those medical facilities were serving, both from a military and civilian perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that in those first few months you travelled around a lot in the area?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I did. During those -- during those first few weeks, I spent quite a lot of my time on the -- on the ground, visiting villages and the town itself, getting to know local people and, in particular, the medical personnel both in the town and in the outlying villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the area that was covered by -- by the B Company, was this the opstina of Gornji Vakuf or was it a wider area?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was -- it was predominantly the opstina of Gornji Vakuf, but it did extend outside of those boundaries. For example, we had visit -- opportunity or cause to visit the village of -- of Here, which I understand sat within the Prozor opstina rather than Gornji Vakuf, and we also had cause -- or meetings, for example, in Bugojno also.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you would travel around in the area, what was your general impression about -- about the area as far as it was affected by the war against the Serbs? Did you witness a lot of destruction in the area?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: When we first arrived in Gornji Vakuf, it struck me as a town that was reasonably prosperous compared with some of the communities we'd driven through on our way up. I was -- I remember recalling that there was evidence of quite a lot of new buildings, particularly housing, being put up. There was quite -- there was quite a lively community in the centre of town, with shops open, cafes frequented by young -- young adults, children playing in the streets. There were cars driving around, and there was a -- an air of -- air of relative normality. In those early days I do not recall seeing any what I would call war damage from small arms or heavier weapon systems in Gornji Vakuf or surrounding villages at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. And which ethnic groups were living in the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf was very much a mixed community of Muslims and Croat families, and as -- and the time that we were there in those early -- early few weeks, we were made well aware that this was traditionally a very happy, mixed community with a large number of mixed marriages. And certainly when you spoke to lots of the children, they really didn't have any idea from -- where they came from ethnically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were there many -- were there Serbs in the area as well?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I was not aware of any Serbs in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, yes, you touched upon it already a little bit as far as the relationship between the local Muslims and the Croats is concerned. So you're saying in this first period you didn't feel that there was any tension between those two groups?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Not when we first arrived. As we approached the back end, the last end of -- the last bit of sort of December, 1992, it became increasingly evident that relationships were deteriorating between the two ethnic groups, both in the town and in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how was this noticeable?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Examples would include a lot of the ladies who -- Muslim ladies were now seen wearing more traditional Muslim-style dress, including even younger ladies, whereas previously it had been -- you saw it a little bit in the older ladies, but now it was often in girls and teenagers and in their early 20s. We had evidence of less vehicle movement. The cafes had become noticeably quieter and often empty. The shops were much quieter, and we had stories of, and I personally had firsthand experience of people telling me that they were no longer able to meet with friends from the other ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were there difficulties for Croats or Muslims to -- to buy goods in a shop which was owned by the opposite ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Very much so. We had stories from people that we'd got to know whereby they'd always bought their bread, for example, from a particular bakery, and that was now no longer available to them because it was on the wrong side of the ethnic divide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And this gradual division, was there a distinction on how it developed in Gornji Vakuf town and the villages compared to the villages surrounding Gornji Vakuf town?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: When we'd -- when we'd first arrived, some of the villages were either purely Muslim villages or purely Croat villages, but many of them were -- were mixed and had no particular end of the village, east or west, north or south, that was affiliated by either ethnic group. But towards the end of December, 1992, there was -- it was noticeable that locals were moving within their village to ethnic groupings, or -- or moving to a more ethnically aligned village. So, for example, if you lived in a -- in a mixed Muslim-Croat village, you might well choose to move down or up the hill to a Muslim village if you were a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving up a little bit, you know, towards -- towards the end of December, so you've testified that tensions increased, were there any particular incidents that further, I would say, ignited these tensions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Two incidents that spring to mind about evidence to us of increasing tension, the first of which was New Year's Eve, 1992. The office commander in B Company, Major Alistair Rule, had chosen to invite the two local military commanders, namely the BiH and HVO commander, for dinner that evening. We had in the camp discussed whether we would choose Christmas for the dinner, but decided that that was ethnically sensitive. We had understood that both the commanders would be coming for dinner, but in fact one of them did not turn up. I do not recall who didn't come, but what I do recall is that he said that he didn't feel able to sit down with his counterpart from the opposite ethnic group even in the company of the neutral UNPROFOR base and surrounded by UNPROFOR personnel. The second incident I recall was, in my memory, after that, so probably the first week of 1993 when the -- it was an incident over the raising of a flag. My memory is that that was a BiH flag that was raised either within an HVO predominant area or next to an HVO flag. I cannot quite recall what that was about. As a result of which that caused immense anger and resulted in the BiH flag being torn down and set fire to. And as any of us would appreciate, burning your national flag is a very emotive subject. As a result of that, tensions became immensely increased to the point that Major Rule had cause to bring in the two local commanders to try and defuse the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How -- how did you learn about this incident with the flag? From whom did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I heard that from other military -- UNPROFOR British military BritBat personnel in the camp. I wasn't actually on the ground at that time. In that -- really from the beginning of January, I had finished my tour of getting to know the ground, and with tensions becoming increasingly difficult in the opstina, it was felt more appropriate for me to be in the base at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I would like the witness now to be shown Exhibit 01068.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This will take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you see this document now?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You can see it now. Now, first of all, do you recognise this document? You know what it is?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It's the kind -- the daily infosums that are intelligence summaries that are sent from the operations room of a location up to higher formations. So these would go from Gornji Vakuf up to battle group headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know who would prepare these daily insums?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: They would be prepared on behalf of the officer commanding, so on behalf of Major Rule, by one of two people, either the ops-officer, operations officer, who is Captain Robbie Boyd 1 Royal Irish, or on occasions by the intelligence colour sergeant, who also worked in the operations room, who was, I believe, was called Colour Sergeant Williams, who was again 1 Cheshire cap badged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, with this particular document, I'd like to focus your attention to the third paragraph, and maybe you could read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: "At approximately 1500 hours on Monday afternoon --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Read it --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Oh, to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You can read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, this report talks about the fact that the HVO raised a Ustasha flag in town, and I think your testimony was that it was the BiH who raised the flag. Would this be a different incident, or do you think that this is the same incident?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, madam. The question, the way it's posed, calls for speculation. "Do you think ..." He can just ask the question whether she knows, not whether she -- I don't think we should be speculating at this point in time, because there may be more than one incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would this be the same incident that you have been referring to? And I -- let me just first -- what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We would need to go back to up the -- to the top. It's a little unclear, but looks like 06-Jan-93.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would this be the same incident as you just had been referring to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: As I -- as I think I alluded to when I described the incident, A, I was not actually on the ground to witness it myself; and secondly, after 12, 13 years, my memory's not entirely accurate as to the exact details. What I do recall is that it was -- in my memory it was very much BiH, but I'm only aware -- aware of the one flag-raising incident, so I would be -- I would believe that that is the incident to which I referred and that I was incorrect in the recollection of which side had raised the flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when the conflict broke out, the date?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I do not know -- I do not recall the exact date. However, I do know that Corporal Edwards was killed on the 13th of January, 1993, and that the fighting had been going for a very small number of days before that incident. And I do also recall that the flag-raising incident occurred very shortly before the outbreak of hostilities in Gornji Vakuf. So I put the date somewhere between the 7th and the -- let's say the 11th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did you personally notice that the conflict had started?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: From my own personal experience, this was my first operational tour, and I had little experience of the firing of variety of weapons all at the same time. We got used, in that time, to rounds of AK-47 bullets being fired off, and that became part of normal daily life to hear that, but all of a sudden the intensity and complexity of the barrage of weapon sounds that we heard was clearly much more than just random AK-47 rounds and appeared to be consolidated bouts of small-arms fire in addition to the introduction and first, from my own experience, first sounds for real of heavier weapon systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In those first few days that the conflict had started, did you remain on the compound or did you actually go outside as well?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I remained in the compound for the first few days of the fighting and, in fact, did not deploy out of our base until the shooting of Corporal Edwards on the 13th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've been twice referring now to the shooting of Corporal Edwards. Could you explain to the Court what happened when Corporal -- Corporal Edwards was shot at.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The -- our UNPROFOR base was approached by a civilian from a local Muslim area, saying that they had a female casualty who was severely ill and in respiratory distress who required moving to a Muslim medical facility and they were unable to, A, treat her in their own community; and secondly, were unable to move her freely and without risk to her. And we -- it was made clear to her that that would be -- for us to move her would be in breach of our mandate, but Major Rule did agree that we -- we, the UNPROFOR forces, would escort their vehicle. To that end, he requested that I accompany that escort duty, travelling in the front Warrior. The convoy became lead Warrior with myself as a passenger, the -- the casualty's vehicle with the lady in it, and a rear Warrior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you for one second. You've been referring to a Warrior. Can you explain what a Warrior is.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It's an infantry armoured fighting personnel carrier. So it looks like a mini tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We left the base about 10.30 that morning. It was the first time I'd been out on the ground. We didn't -- the -- the town was quiet, immensely quiet, eerily quiet, and to that end the vehicle was what we called the mortar hatches were open; in other words, we were in the back of the vehicle, actually stood up so you can actually see all around. We drove, and as we approached the crossroads in centre of Gornji Vakuf we realised the rear vehicle had swerved into the bridge, and that was because the driver had sustained a gunshot wound to his face, wound -- bullet exiting out of the rear of his brain, and he was, for all intents and purposes, killed instantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you do when this happened?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The -- as I say, the front vehicle immediately reversed to ascertain what had happened. The -- the vehicle carrying the Muslim casualty had disappeared. I have no idea what happened to that. We then what we call militarily, de-bused, got out of the vehicle, and assisted in extracting Corporal Wayne Edwards from his driver's seat, which was difficult because, in the crash, the electrics had failed so we weren't able to pull the seat back and he was a fairly large gentleman, and we then carried out cardiopulmonary resuscitation and other lifesaving techniques in the lee of the bridge for some protection for ourselves. He was then -- I called up for -- I didn't -- I requested that one of our ambulances came out, A, to provide me with assistance, and B, to extract the casualty back to the base. At that time I knew that he -- he was dead, but I wasn't going to certify him dead in the middle of the -- at the side of a river. I felt that it was more appropriate to return to base and -- and to do the necessary medicolegal checks to certify him dead when we were back in camp some 30 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know from which direction the shot came from that -- that hit the corporal?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Immediately after the -- as I -- just -- as I'd said, it was eerily quiet as we went into town. There was nobody around at all, and there was no noise. So to hear a couple of rounds of small arms go off was very noticeable. And on hearing those, looked up to the direction in which I'd thought the rounds had come, and looked up and to the right of the crossroads and saw what I believed to be two guys with a weapon stood in an open window in a block of -- in a modern block of flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were these guys arrested afterwards, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
