utterances.text: There was a British military investigation into this incident, and I understand that there was outrage from both BiH and HVO command on the ground, and as a result of which an investigation was attempted. I don't believe that anybody was -- was arrested. The hearsay or similar that we got was that these were two previously known criminal brothers of Croat extraction who'd probably used the war as an opportunity to continue some of their criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you were driving through Gornji Vakuf town, you said there was an eerie silence. Was there any damage to buildings in the area that you were driving through?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was a noticeably different vista than I had seen previously. The drive from our factory complex to the crossroads where the shooting took place was through what was Muslim community, and it was -- it was a marked amount of damage to civilian houses that I noticed. The hotel which had sat on the crossroads was all but razed to the ground, and what had been the town's main medical centre on the left as you drove in had also received a not insignificant amount of battle damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 01113.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Carter, once this document appears on your screen, I'd like to ask you to read for yourself the first paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would this report reflect what you've just testified to us?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Again, it's not awfully clear to read but looks like "13 Jan 93."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It looks like something "Jan 93."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Once the conflict had started, did there come a time after the start of the conflict that you were taking up another function?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: As the fighting intensified, Major -- the officer commanding was approached by UNHCR and IRC as to whether, in view of the intensity of the fighting, we - we UNPROFOR - could assist in carrying out some of the tasks that they were supposed to be undertaking, because they were unable to do so. As a result of that request, a meeting was held in the UNPROFOR base with representatives from both of those organisations to look at what, if anything, we could do in order to stay within our own mandate and -- and theirs. OC B Company was clearly was fully occupied controlling the military aspects of the deployment, and the OC of the workshops was fully occupied in keeping the vehicles on the road. And thankfully, we were not ourselves busy, and as such it was proposed and accepted that, as the other senior officer in the camp, that I should take on that role, and it also sat comfortably insofar as I'd already been out and about to the villages, met the local sort of humanitarian representative in each village, and had a feel as to the ethnicity of villages and number of people living in those villages. So both agencies were happy that I could take that on as a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So -- so what was the result of this? What -- what did they ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: They --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'm referring now to IRC and UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. They asked if we would be involved in the delivery of food packages, the cardboard food parcels, and plastic sheeting for replacing roofs and windows, because obviously in the middle of winter that was an important part of their support to -- to towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And for how long did you -- did you take up this -- this task?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We took up the task only for a short period of time. They delivered approximately 20 tons of aid to us and 20 tons of aid covering -- covering such a large community doesn't -- doesn't go very far and doesn't last very long, and as a matter of fact, we never needed to take any resupply from them because they -- the situation became such that they felt that they were able to -- to take it back on. So we did it for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- I'm sorry, may I just ask a question of understanding? What does IRC stand for? You referred to IRC. It's not ICRC, by the way, the International Committee of the Red Cross. No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. It's an American --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: International Relief --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Committee, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've forgotten my question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My question was that you said that you took up this task for a short period of time, and my question is how long was this short period of time?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Oh, some five -- five days, seven days, 10 days, something of that nature. It was a very short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you transport this -- this aid to the villages?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The aid was transported nearly always in the backs of my armoured ambulance, the 432, to which I've previously referred. Very occasionally we would use the Warrior fighting vehicle, the Warrior armoured personnel carriers for that purpose, but predominantly it was in the back of the 432s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how would this in practice work when you distribute this in the village? Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes. We would go invariably as a secondary tasking. The taskings would be given by the OC as to where he needed to have troops on the ground, and invariably we would then be invited to accompany that patrol. Thinking out in the villages, that would then involve quite a lot of cross -- crossing of checkpoints to get to where we were going, and often crossing from HVO territory into BiH and back into HVO or whatever, and so it was often quite a lengthy process. And invariably by the time we arrived in whichever village we were going to, the local village commander was aware that we were coming, presumably from messages from the checkpoints that we'd driven through. And it was then a case of meeting with the local humanitarian village commander to ascertain, from my perspective, what requirements they had with regard to what casualties they'd suffered within the community, what -- whether they'd had houses damaged and as to whether they needed plastic sheeting, for example. And as we'd already decided ourselves, but also in line with the UNHCR and IRC, it was very much on a 50/50 distribution. So the distribution was not based upon request for perceived need by them or by us. It was very much 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in your opinion, were both ethnic groups also in equal need for this humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: There was pre- -- before the fighting started, there was already evidence that there was discrepancy between the - I'm not sure - we call stock holdings of food and medical supplies on both sides of the divide, but as the fighting intensified and the damage to Muslim-controlled areas appeared to be greater, the -- the discrepancy between the need became exaggerated, became more evident with the need on the Muslim side being greater than on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you said already before the start of the conflict, you know, in looking at the stockpiles, it appeared that the Croats would have more supplies than the Muslims. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The -- the locals themselves, before the fighting started, had spoken to us about the fact that everybody had feared that war was inevitable and that people had started to do their stockpiling in anticipation of conflict. Because of fighting elsewhere and the large movements of refugees around Central Bosnia, the Muslim communities were reporting that they'd had larger number of refugees come to live in the Gornji Vakuf opstina than -- than the Croats had and, therefore, the communities which might have been, say, 50, if a village had been 50 pre-movement of personnel, it might now have risen to a hundred. And so when you'd stockpiled for 50 and you suddenly had a hundred, it wasn't going to go far enough. Another example that the locals gave us from both sides was that the Croat communities were quite heavily subsidised or supported from Croatia, and also from Germany, whereas the BiH and the Muslim families did not report having -- feeling that they had support from anywhere, and -- and used to touch upon the feelings that they didn't have support from the wider Muslim world, partly because of the type of Muslim religion that they had in recent years followed. There was also -- before the fighting started, I'd had, as part of my understanding of the ground, had opportunity to visit both Caritas and Merhamet in Gornji Vakuf centre, and it was evident there that both communities had reasonably well-stocked warehouses actually in Gornji Vakuf. I certainly saw -- I personally saw lots of Caritas wagons, I rarely saw Merhamet, but Merhamet must have been getting there to supply the warehouses. But that wasn't the case when you got out into the rural communities where there seemed to be much more of a divide. And we tried to ascertain whether that was a distribution problem or whether there was difficulties with them actually getting into their own villages, and we did have reports that at checkpoints, HVO checkpoints, the food was -- or the distributions from -- by Merhamet were being confiscated. But -- and obviously all of -- all of those various parts went towards causing a discrepancy in two similar sized villages from the different ethnic divides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would that also be, I mean, a reason why that -- well, let me ask you this: Was there a difference in the general standard of living between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: There was. Pre -- pre the fighting, not a hundred per cent by any stroke of the imagination, but there was evidence that on the whole the Croat communities were more affluent than the Muslim communities, as I say, not by least -- by any means was that unanimous. And it was often around the more luxury end of goods. For example, the numbers of current models of TVs, videos, fridges, microwave ovens were more evident in Croat households than in Muslim households.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, while you were travelling around in -- during the conflict in January and February, 1993, to these various villages, did you ever get opportunities to talk to the local villagers?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I had lots of opportunities throughout my tour to -- to talk to local villagers. Invariably that was through interpreters, be they UNPROFOR-employed interpreters or the military interpreter, and just occasionally when we were on the ground without either, several of my soldiers are German speakers, or were German speakers, and that was quite often a language of -- the mutual language we could communicate in, and we came across, of course, people who spoke potted English, and we'd learnt the odd word or two of local language as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what would these villagers -- what kind of stories would these villagers tell you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Before -- before the fighting broke out or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, after the fighting had broken out.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Once the fighting had broken out, the common theme from both Croat families and from Muslim families was the disbelief as to the level of hatred that had now arisen in such a short space of time and the feeling that they, as local people, did not want the war and the fighting to continue. And that, as I say, came from both -- both sides. With regard to describing suffering and disturbing stories, they were predominantly from the Muslim families that we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What kind of disturbing stories would -- would they --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may intervene. The witness's evidence does have to have some showing of probative value here, and so far we're having stories related from people who haven't even been identified through a medium of interpretation, sometimes British soldiers speaking a level of German that we haven't even been told about. Your Honour, there should be some showing of probative value for all of this rather than just a generalised relating of the -- of these undefined stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Would you try and ask more precise questions, please, because if we remain at the level of generalities, we won't get far.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I was getting to that, Your Honours, and I will do right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you -- do you recall a specific conversation that you had with a young lady about in her 20s?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I spoke with a young -- a young lady, a young Muslim lady in her early 20s, who lived in a rural community. She was from that village and was not originally from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this village?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this -- excuse me, madam. At this point I'm going to object to hearing the rest of this story. One, we don't know the name of this individual, unless it can be recalled; and two, we don't know the name of the place, so we need a little bit more. But I think, how is it possible for the Defence to challenge evidence of this nature? Albeit this Tribunal does allow quite a bit of hearsay, I think now it's a little bit so far removed that it makes it impossible for the Defence to challenge such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Try and have the witness speak more specifically, give us an idea of the village she met this young lady in, and things like that. Thank you. Was it within 15 minutes of where she was, or half an hour, two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard what the Judge said. Can you be a bit more specific about where, in which village this was? Would you recall anything more specific?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I can't recall the -- I can't recall the name of the village. What I do recall is some -- some idea of where within the opstina, and I apologise for those who don't know the roads to which I refer in Gornji Vakuf, but if you come to the crossroads in the centre of the town and turn right as if you were going towards Bugojno, and the -- once you've left the outskirts of the -- the town, and then turn right up into the hills along there, and the village was a reasonable way up sort of windy rural -- rural roads. The travel time from the base was in the region of 20 to 30 minutes' drive, but allowing for that, some of that was through roughly roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this a Muslim village or a Croat village or a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So please continue. I don't know where you left off, but you were talking to this girl, and what did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: She described how the previous night she had been awoken to find a number - two or three - unknown males in her room who she took to be HVO soldiers because of the dress that they were wearing and the insignia that they had on. She was then -- she then described that she was raped by these soldiers and that she'd been prevented from screaming by them covering her mouth. There were other ladies living in the house at the time, and she was not aware whether any others had been raped. When I was speaking to her, she was clearly upset. She was dressed in Muslim dress, and I appreciate I do not know her name. I don't believe I even asked her her name at the time. She was in her early 20s. She had long plaits, and she was forever taking her headsquare off and playing with her plaits and putting it back on, which I took to be part of her anxiety. She was comforted by a much older lady who I took to be a relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you speak with her in English or did she --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I was working through one of our UNPROFOR female interpreters, and on that occasion, as was quite often the case, it was an all-female environment, insofar as that although I had male soldiers and drivers with me, they invariably stayed outside to let the young children in the village climb all over the vehicles and just play, and they were protecting the vehicles as well. So quite often it was all ladies in the room with a female interpreter, because both of our UNPROFOR interpreters were female, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, did you report on this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you report in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- it was not -- not the modus operandus of B Company to report things in writing. They were given as verbal reports back to the chain of command, either the ops-officer or the officer commanding, and it was left for them to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And do you know what was the consequence of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular incident I do not. It was very often that when I came -- when we'd been out on the ground, not only myself but other people reporting incidents back, if there were incidents of concern, then the officer commanding would organise to meet with either, either, or both of the local commanders in order to ascertain their understanding of stories that we had been given by -- from the locals that we'd met on our trips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you yourself follow up on this story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I did not follow up on this story other than, as I say, to report it back to the chain -- to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this part of the examination-in-chief and this story about the rape has no place here, it should be redacted from the transcript, because the incident is not mentioned in the indictment nor the paragraphs quoted as being relevant paragraphs, nor does rape exist in the indictment, rape in Vakuf, Gornji Vakuf or, rather, the Vakuf municipality or opstina. That does not exist in the indictment. We have been taken by surprise. We did not conduct an investigation into any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I turn to the Prosecution. The Defence has said that rape in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf is not included in the indictment. So would you continue your examination on important points, but if this is not in the indictment, or perhaps you're laying grounds for a question that you're going to ask in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reason why I led this evidence is because of paragraph 60 -- 67 in the indictment, which talks about the general attack on the villages in Gornji Vakuf, and which says that "during their detention, Muslim men, women, children and elderly were kept in harsh conditions and often mistreated and/or abused." And it's particularly to this paragraph that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mistreatment and abuse of civilians in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can all read and we can call read the paragraph, but I still don't see the crime of rape in that paragraph. It cannot come under the description as it is presented here. So that is our standing objection, objection to the unclear form of the indictment. That's my first point. And in paragraph 66, if we look at the annex following on from this, then we see the locations, and in view of the objection made by my colleague, my learned colleague, we don't know where this happened, so the Defence cannot prepare for this. It cannot conduct an investigation into the incident before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 67 there are four localities; Dusa, Hrasnica and the other two places. I apologise for the poor pronunciation. Dusa, Hrasnica, Uzricje and Zdrimci. And it goes on to speak of plunder and burnt houses. Now, I'm going to ask the witness or you can ask her whether she saw burnt houses, destroyed houses, and whether the woman in question spoke about -- referred to any of this. So we have paragraph 67 where the places are mentioned. So would you focus on the question and the answer. We're either losing time or we can focus on the heart of the matter. But perhaps we'll see where you're -- this is leading to with the follow-up questions. Otherwise, I'll ask the questions myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll move on to a -- I was finished with this topic anyway. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were you also involved in the distribution of medical supplies to various medical centres in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: During the -- during the -- during the time, we were involved in having an understanding of the medical capability within the town and within the villages, but the issue of distribution of medical supplies rested quite firmly with Medecins sans Frontieres and Pharmaciens sans Frontieres, and as such we didn't actually distribute medical supplies, but I had an understanding of what was available to various medical facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you visit the medical facilities in Gornji Vakuf town, the Muslim and Croat medical centres during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: During -- during the conflict I had cause to visit both the main medical centres for the HVO Croat population and the BiH Muslim communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you explain a little bit about -- could you explain what -- what about the situation was in both of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Starting with the -- with the medical centre in the Muslim side, their main medical centre was located in a converted house. It had been converted quite late because the main medical centre in the centre of town was predominantly in -- if I understand to be a Muslim area, and the medical facility was now based around normal household equipment. For example, there were no hospital beds, they were the kind of beds that you would have found in a normal home. There were, for example, beds squashed in together. Say there were five -- five or six beds squashed together in what had been a room, but on one occasion I recall going and visiting, and in order to get sufficient casualties on the beds, the casualties were actually laid sort of the other way, and so in fact there were getting on twice as many casualties as there were number of beds, if that makes sense. There was no store facility as such and the medical supplies were stored in what had been the kitchen cupboards and living-room cupboards. The supplies were very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how was this facility compared to the Croat medical centre?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The Croat medical centre, the main medical centre in Gornji Vakuf was based in the crypt of a large church. It was a very spacious facility including having a dedicated surgical capability, insofar as, if I remember correctly, right deep in the -- in the church, a room which had two proper surgical tables, is my recollection, with dedicated surgical lighting. I don't recall whether that was hospital-style surgical lighting or just use of civilian lighting appropriately positioned. The storerooms were exceedingly well -- exceedingly well stocked. I remember being shown into a very large storeroom with shelving and supplies floor to ceiling. The -- they had quite a number of medical staff from their -- from the local area. I remember particularly meeting the female gynaecologist who was from Gornji Vakuf herself, and I also remember meeting a dental officer who actually didn't come from Gornji Vakuf, came from somewhere considerably north, outside of the -- outside of the whole area, but he'd moved there for family -- for family reasons, to be closer to his own family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: During this period, January, February, 1993, when you went around in the area, did you ever notice any damages to property in the villages that you -- that you visited?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: There was extensive damage to property throughout the area, but by far and away to Muslim communities. There was lots of villages that were, for all intents and purposes, completely destroyed, where 90, 95 per cent of houses were -- were now uninhabitable. And -- and in reference to one of the comments from -- from the Judges earlier, I am aware of -- of houses that were -- that were burnt as part of the conflict as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've mentioned destruction of houses. Was there also other property? Did you also witness other property that was damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- invariably in a community the religious centre of the village, be that the church or -- or the mosque, would have some evidence of -- of damage, but I do not recall ever seeing a church tower damaged other than superficial splats from munition strikes. However, I do remember vividly seeing minarets that were destroyed quite often with the metal structure that sits inside to hold the -- hold the tower up exposed and bent, and often the minaret actually sort of toppled over. And I also do not recall ever seeing damage to Christian graveyards, but I do recall damage to Muslim graveyards with knocking over of headstones, graffiti, and used as a sort of pivo throwing away area. Often lots of cans and bottles of beer in the graveyards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you've been referring to destroyed minarets and mosque, can you think of any particular villages?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I recall -- the one that strikes in my mind is probably the village of Bastrica, for two reasons: It was close to us. It was a village we'd been to regularly. It was a village where the -- there was a sniper working out of the church tower who was pinning down local Muslims, and ourselves too, made it quite difficult for us to operate in Bastrica. In the church, less small arms damage was -- the tower was very much standing whereas the minaret in Bastrica was closer to horizontal than vertical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was there a difference in the type of destruction you observed in Gornji Vakuf town and the villages you observed in the opstina?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I think in the -- in the town, the -- the damage to -- to property was much more that which would be attributable to the rigors of war fighting, be from small arms and larger munitions, artillery shells, for example, landing on roofs and sides of buildings. Whereas although there was evidence of that to a lesser extent in the outlying villages, the damage seemed much more to be related to houses being burnt and left uninhabitable from that rather than the house half falling down or the roof falling in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you visited these villages and noted this destruction, were reports made about this type of destruction, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Once again, when -- after every trip out there was a requirement to provide a briefing back to the operations room and/or the officer commanding, and to report what you -- what one had found on the ground, conversations you'd had with military and civilian personnel, to talk about how easy it was or not easy to get to the place, to provide grid references of checkpoints and, therefore, as part of that would be to describe the -- the state of property within the village or villages we had visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How detailed would these reports be as far as destruction is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It would be -- it would usually be along the lines of giving a -- an estimate as to the percentage of damage, the type of damage, and any significant structures that had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was anything particular noticeable in the villages where -- in mixed villages where both Muslims and Croats would live, as far as destruction is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: With regard to the destruction, it was markably noticeable, the difference between the amount of destruction on the Muslim side compared to the Croat side, with the Muslim side being considerably more noticeably damaged. Again, Bastrica springs to mind. The -- I had with me a -- an SLR camera with a wide-angle lens, and I had a photograph of the centre of Bastrica, being able to get sufficiently far away to get both sides, and the BiH side is in effect razed to the ground, whereas the -- the -- the Croat side is -- is -- is much -- it is damaged but much less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, we've spoken a lot about destruction in the village, and I'm going to ask you now do you recall any names of any particular Muslim villages that stood out as being heavily destructed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- there are five or six villages' names that have stuck with me since -- since my tour, and I guess at the time there were many, many more villages, the names of which I knew off the back of my hand, but the villages that have stuck in my mind are the villages of Bastrica, Dusa, Hrasnica, Uzricje and Zdrimci. I apologise if the pronunciation of those is not helpful. I also remember Vrse and I think I remember that because it was one of the easier ones to say and only had four letters in its name, whereas the others were quite difficult for my non-linguistic English tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm noting the time. I don't know if we need a break now or we need to continue for a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue for another ten minutes. You have ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 01373. I'd request that the second page of this report to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read -- read for yourself the paragraphs numbered as A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I've read those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've been referring to the villages of Zdrimci and Vrse, which have been referred to in this report. Is -- the report on the destruction of the houses in this particular report, does that correspond with your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we at least establish what this document is and whether the witness has any knowledge of it before she's asked questions about it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I could do that, Your Honours. If we can move to the first page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I do indeed. The previous -- I think it was the previous document I was asked to look at, talking about Corporal Edwards' death, was a B Company milinfosum. Those company milinfosums are then consolidated by the operations officer of the Cheshire's Battle Group in Vitez and form then a Cheshire's Battle Group milinfosum which is then sent to higher formations. So this is a conglomeration of the various company reports from the -- from the date stated. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what is the date stated?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: 31st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we can move again to the second page. And, yeah, I had already asked. Is the reporting on the destruction of these villages, is that in concurrence with your experience in the field?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. That's very much as -- as my experiences were on -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 01600, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, what kind of document is this? Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Again, it's from the 3rd of March, 1993, and it's the 1 Cheshire's Battle Group milinfosum, and therefore covers the reports from not only B Company's AOR - areas of responsibility - but also the areas of responsibility of the other Cheshire companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe -- could you read out loud for us paragraphs A and B of this report.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: "The village of Uzice, grid reference 068666 had 80 per cent of its housing destroyed by external HVO/HOS troops during the ethnic conflict. The only houses remaining in the village are predominantly -- are reportedly Croat houses." Paragraph Bravo: "The hamlet of Dusa grid reference 070672 formerly 100 per cent Muslim has been totally destroyed. Only one old man is now believed to be living in the village." Paragraph Charlie --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Alpha and Bravo is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, this may be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at approximately ten to six, and we will shall be working until 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1386, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at this document and tell me whether you recognise this document. Oh, sorry. It was still the old one.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it as a 1 Cheshire milinfosum, dated the 1st of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Move to page 2, please. Witness, I'm interested in the second part -- paragraph, and I'd like you to read out the last sentence of this second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: "There has been extensive damage to many Muslim villages, including the almost total destruction of the village of Hrasnica which has obviously created much fresh hatred toward the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this the name of the village that you mentioned earlier as one of the villages that had extensive destruction?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was one of the villages that I named earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was -- another village that you mentioned earlier was the village of Dusa. Did you ever visit the village of Dusa?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I did visit the village of Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know when you visited?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. I visited Dusa in -- once the fighting had started, towards the end -- towards the end of January, 1993. I don't remember the exact -- the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember the reason why you visited Dusa?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not recall why -- why we were going to Dusa, but as I previously stated, it would have been under the direction of OC B Company rather than of my own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell me what -- what happened when you -- when you visited this village.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: As we -- as we came into the village, we were met by a very distressed community, and in particular we were met by somebody who spoke a little bit of broken English, but -- and therefore was trying to tell us the story in English, but we -- we actually had an interpreter with us, so we were able to communicate through an UNPROFOR interpreter and not rely on his broken -- their broken command of English. And the story we were given was that the village had been attacked by HVO soldiers - it was a Muslim village - and that the women, children, and elderly men had been herded into the two houses that were sitting, as we drove in, on the right-hand side of the village. They were partially constructed. Partially constructed. Very nearly finished, but partly constructed houses. And in the process of the attack, the men of fighting age, including some that, we were reported, were probably slightly too young to be counted as fighters and slightly too old to be counted as fighters but nevertheless had been counted as fighting age, had been herded up and the majority of them forced into the backs of trucks to be taken away. When we asked as to where they believed them to be taken, they had no idea, although they said that they feared that they would be taken away to detention facilities and that in fact that would be less preferable to them being taken away and killed because the suffering that their menfolk would suffer in a detention facility would be greater than that of being killed. But they also told us about some that had been killed actually in the village whilst they were there but that those bodies had already been taken away by -- by these HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When -- when you say that -- you know, that people had been killed, do you know who had been killed? Did they tell you? Were these Muslim men or civilians, or were they more specific on who was killed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: They told us that it was out of the group of men of fighting age that had been killed but that they were not fighters, and that's why they were still in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you walk around in the village?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We did. We were escorted by the same guy who -- who had met us and were very much under his direction as to where we were -- where we went. From our perspective, that was fine because he'd obviously walked around the village already, and from a military perspective certainly concerned that areas might be booby-trapped or mined and so we were not going to ask to go anywhere where he wasn't prepared to take us. We didn't want to become casualties ourselves. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. What did you notice as you were walking around?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: What he -- what he showed us was -- appeared to be the -- all of the houses within the village. We certainly couldn't see, you know, houses that he didn't show us, if that makes sense. And there were about -- about 20 houses of which all but the two where the women and children were appeared to have been set on fire and -- and destroyed. There was little evidence of munitions damage to the buildings. There was a few impact -- impact marks but nothing of any great note. And it would appear that the incident had happened fairly recently insofar as you could still smell the burning in the air and one or two of the buildings were still not actually alight but were still smouldering.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did the person who guided you around stop at some specific houses?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The house that -- there was one particular house that he wanted us to be made aware of which was towards the left-hand side of the village as we walked round and was about a third of the way into the village, and he told us that men had been forcibly taken into the basement of the building, and that's where he believed that they'd been shot and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you notice about the basement of these -- of these houses?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We didn't go into the basements, for reasons that I've previously described, but because of the lie of the land and the slope and the ground, obviously being on -- not absolutely flat, you could see into the basements, and there was evidence of -- of bloodstaining and what appeared to be, but looking from a distance, human hair, but as I say, looking from -- from a distance. There were no bodies in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And -- and had these houses also been destroyed by fire?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: They had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the basement as well?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you -- are you saying that there were traces of blood which, according to what you saw, in your judgement then were posterior to the burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As -- as -- not that I've -- in my experience when a house is burnt, that you can have areas where it doesn't burn and areas where it does, and so I wouldn't like to say which came first. I wouldn't be forensically in a position to say which preceded the other, the blood or the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, after you visited Dusa, did you ever spoke with some -- a local HVO medic about this?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I did. A day or two later, I -- I was visiting a nearby HVO village very close by. My recollection is that -- if I had a map it would be sort of the adjacent run of villages. As the villages run up and down the hills, adjacent village. Not up and down but sort of across the hillside. Who was an HVO medic, and he asked if I was aware of what had gone on in Dusa, because he'd had cause to tend to some casualties, and he went on it tell me that he could not believe the inhumanity that had been inflicted on the people of Dusa and that he understood that they were fighters from outside of the local Gornji Vakuf area for two reasons, because, A, he didn't recognise any of them, which is what the villagers told us, that they didn't recognise any of the guys who had come in the village, but also that he had been told that that was the case, that the people who had been to Dusa were not Gornji Vakuf personnel but from -- but from elsewhere, although he didn't say from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that -- that he said that he -- that this HVO medic said he couldn't believe the inhumanity that had been inflicted on the people of Dusa. Was -- was this the only thing he said, or was he more specific as to what kind of inhumanity had been inflicted?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He was talking about the brutality of the way in which the people were -- were handled, and the way in which the women and children had been forced to go where they'd been forced to go, the way in which the guys had been -- the -- the male members had been put into the -- into the trucks, and what he described as the murder rather than the killing by fighting of -- of the individuals concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was he more specific about the individuals concerned as to who had been murdered? Because you've also said that he had cause to tend some casualties.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who had been --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He said that they were men. He'd seen -- as casualties, he'd seen people who were trying to run away, to flee away, and not that he'd been part necessarily of the -- of the incident and that they -- that they became -- they became involved sort of as a -- as a subsidiary to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could I ask for some precision here? I'm not a native English speaker, as you hear quite well. The term "casualties," as I understand it, can have several meanings, or does it only refer to people who actually died or also to people who were wounded? And if it has these double -- these double meanings, do you have an idea whether your interlocutor spoke of one or the other or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The term -- the term "casualty" we'd come to use as being those who were injured as opposed to the dead who were the other group, and that's a distinction that's quite clearly and freely made within military speak and reporting, because when we're sending -- when we're sending casualty sitreps from the ground, we quite clearly distinguish between the injured and the dead, and we have a grading to describe -- to describe that. So we were quite clear that a casualty is an injured person, and that does not therefore include the dead. The dead are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've also mentioned the village Uzricje. Did you ever visit Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I did visit Uzricje. Uzricje was one of the villages that often came up in discussions and as an area of concern within B Company's location and therefore was, shall we say, quite often on the visiting rota of villages and, as I say, I was therefore in a position to visit Uzricje as part of the B Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you just visit it just once or on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I visited Uzricje on several occasions. I'd certainly visited Uzricje before the fighting started, so the back end of 1992, and visited it during the period of more intense fighting. And if I remember rightly, I have also been to visit it sort of when it was much quieter and really not very much --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what do you remember of these visits and particularly the ones during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: During -- during the conflict, it was a village that had suffered very badly, and was -- showed evidence of lots of damage to -- to property, again with lots of burnt-out houses rather than -- although still with evidence of munitions damage to houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were Muslims still living in the village?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The village was very -- had very reduced number of inhabitants over the -- over the time that -- that we were visiting. And by the end of the time, it's one of the villages that I remember as being really essentially abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the condition of these Muslims who were still in the villages? What were their living conditions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Living conditions in many of the Muslim villages was dreadful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In particular, in Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was dreadful. The very -- people tending to live together in the houses that were least badly damaged, so living very, very many in one small house, leading very much a hand-to-mouth existence with regard to how much food they had and other sort of staples of life. Like everybody else, they didn't have electricity, but then that was true for everybody, less ourselves and some of the headquarters facilities in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Are you saying that throughout the period of January, February, there was no electricity in any of the villages or Gornji Vakuf town?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: No, no, no. The medical facilities had generators and military establishments, and so command-post type places had generators, but I think the greater the problem than generators was fuel supply for those generators. And one of my abiding memories is looking out and seeing absolutely no lights, and it felt like forever, forgetting what the street lighting or night light looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let's move on to another topic. Did you ever participate in cease-fire meetings or negotiations of cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Because I spent quite a lot of my time out and about on the ground, and because I was aware of some of the, in the broadest sense, humanitarian consequences of the fighting and had been given stories from local villagers of the kinds of events that had gone on in their village, I was on occasions invited to sit in and participate in cease-fire negotiations that were convened and chaired by OC B Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who would be representing the ethnic groups in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Many of the meetings that were held were attended by the local commander from HVO forces and from BiH forces, but there were occasions where commanders from higher formations were in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular meeting where, like you say, commanders from higher formations were in attendance? Do you recall any particular meeting and any particular person who -- who would be a commander of a higher formation?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The one that I remember most vividly was a gentleman I believe to be known as Colonel Siljeg who was from the higher command of HVO forces. I believe he came from Mostar, although I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting in which Colonel Siljeg also participated?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There was one particular meeting around the same sort of time as -- as sort of the back end -- back end of January time. So around the same time as Dusa. I don't remember if it was before or after, but around that sort of time, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember the topics that were discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. There were two main topics that were discussed. One was over the allegations or reports that we'd had from local populations that the HVO were intending to use tankers, petrol tankers from the hillsides outside Gornji Vakuf, to roll them down the hill, set fire to them, with a view to wiping out Muslim communities in order to put a stop to the fighting once and for all and to ethnically --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This was a rumour that -- that --

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That we'd heard, yeah, from quite a lot of sources within the Gornji Vakuf opstina. And at that meeting, there was also debate - I believe it was the same meeting - the debate about body exchange and -- and setting -- setting up body exchanges. I don't believe the body exchange that actually did happen was actually agreed at that meeting. I believe it was initially discussed, and other themes for that meeting. That was the main thing talked about at that meeting. Other themes, again trying to seek clarification about allegations that we'd had about the use of outside -- outside troops to augment HVO fighting capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did Colonel Siljeg say about that particular topic, about whether the -- about the involvement of outside troops in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He -- he denied that HVO forces from elsewhere were -- were coming, but did say that he saw Gornji Vakuf as a main thrust, as we would say in military terms, a main focus for -- for fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The main focus for whom?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: For the HVO. And it was one of their central objectives, I guess, would be the military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did anything particular happen at that meeting as far as Mr. Siljeg was concerned that -- that kept in your mind?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. At that particular meeting, it was a very disjointed meeting insofar as Colonel Siljeg continued to receive numerous telephone calls into our operations room downstairs. The meetings were held in the officers' mess room upstairs, and Colonel Siljeg was forever getting calls in the ops room and so breaking the meeting, going downstairs and taking the call, and coming back upstairs, and a short while later getting another call and going back down and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever say whom he had to call?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. He reported that he was talking to his higher formation and that during the course of the -- of these telephone calls up and down he was very pleased to inform everybody present, ourselves and the BiH, that much as we'd been giving him a hard time and suggesting that things were not as they should be, he'd been congratulated by his higher formation and had actually been -- and I don't remember whether his words were rewarded, congratulated, promoted, or something along those lines, and was very proud and pleased to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how did you interpret the fact that he was so proud and pleased to -- to inform the other participants of the meeting that he had -- that he had been promoted?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He -- it -- it came -- it came across as -- and again this may be an English term, that he was giving a two fingers up to -- a less pleasant sign, to -- to the rest of us, that he was very much in the right and that he was -- he was being recognised for his military prowess and that stuff the rest of us, he and his -- he and his command would continue to behave and continue their military planning and operations in the direction of which they were -- or he was intent, and that had the backing -- and that had the backing of his higher command and wasn't him just acting on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How would you describe the general demeanour of Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He's -- he stands out in my mind as a very memorable individual, both with regard to his very bushy eyebrows, which joined in the middle and his very deep-set dark eyes, and he had a very commanding presence, but associated with that was very much a man of arrogance and self-belief and very pompous, and -- and that came across both in his body language but also in the way -- in the way in which he would address the meeting, be that addressing us or his opposite number or in fact his own HVO subordinate commanders too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this the only time you met Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That's the only recollection I have of actually sitting in a meeting with him. I do know that he visited the base on more than one occasion, but as I say, that was the only meeting that I recall sitting in with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness -- could the witness be shown Exhibit 01351 [Realtime transcript read in error "01531"], please. And could the witness be shown the English version of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think there is mistake in the notes. It says here in the notes 01531 and I think it's 01351.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: 01351, yes. I think the exhibit which is on the screen is the document but in the original language. There we go. There's the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you describe what you -- what you see at this document, what kind of document it appears to be?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It looks like -- it looks like an official document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness should not, with all due respect, speculate about what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Either she knows the document or not. If not, well, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could be shown the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you see the name that appears at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It's commander Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, which is how I -- I -- the middle name -- the personal name I wouldn't recognise, but -- but the other I read as the gentleman I knew as Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. And could the witness now be shown page 3 of the English version of the document. Could you read this page and -- and tell the Court whether you recognise any of the names of the villages that are mentioned in this -- on this page.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: From -- from the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, you don't have to read it out loud. Just read the document and tell me whether you recognise any of the names of the villages.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Just as I'm reading it down, Uzricje I've already mentioned, Dusa I recognise, we've already spoken about that, Trnovaca likewise. Luzani doesn't ring a bell, and Gornji Ricica does ring a bell but not as much as the first three. So the first of that one, two, three, four, about sort of the top paragraph, the first -- the first three I recognise as -- very much so. The fourth one I don't, and the fifth -- the fifth one I do but less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if we just move -- scroll to the bottom of the page. Could you read out what's -- what's in red under -- under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect, I don't know what probative value this could possibly have. The witness has said that she has no knowledge of this document beyond speculating that it looks like an official document, and having her read out the contents has no probative value whatsoever and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness knows about what -- she has given testimony about what has happened in these villages and she has given testimony about the person, Colonel Siljeg, which she knows, and for that reason I'm showing her this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Judges are of the opinion that she cannot confirm the document, but on the other hand, you can say to her, you said a moment ago such-and-such and I see the contrary in the document, for example, and then you could ask her for an explanation. But otherwise speaking, this is a document drafted by this colonel. The witness has never seen it. All she can say is that she went to some of these villages where she was able to make certain observations. So you can confront those observations with the contents of the document if there are any differences. In any case, that would be useful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that was my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then get to the heart of the matter quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, just -- so reading again the bottom of the page under number 4, could you please read that out loud.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Number 4 states: "A total of 24 houses destroyed (22 torched, 2 shelled)."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's been written there, is that -- of course -- does that correspond with your observations as regards the destruction?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We then move to page 5, please. And again I would like you to scroll down to the bottom of this page. And could you again read out what's been written under number 4.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Number 4: "A total of 18 houses and sheds were destroyed, of which 16 were torched and two houses were destroyed by shelling."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And again, the same question, does that correspond with your observations as regards the destruction of Dusa?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever notice any evidence from the field that outside HVO troops were actually involved in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I had two personal incidents that led me to believe that outside HVO forces were involved. The first was the reports on the attack on Dusa, both from the villagers themselves and the HVO medic that we have already discussed, and the second was when I was working down in Tomislavgrad and had cause to go and treat some casualties from a bus incident very close to a British military location called Redoubt Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what happened on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: On that particular occasion we were called to go and assist our own medical -- small medical facility there at the Redoubt Camp following a hand grenade accidentally being discharged on a bus which contained approximately 50 HVO fighters. It was about 0300 hours and was exceedingly cold outside, as I remember reminding my driver we mustn't become casualties ourselves in trying to drive too fast on the ice and snow-packed roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember what time this was?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was about 0300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, but the date.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: The date must have been a little bit later than those incidents that we had been talking about insofar as I was based in Tomislavgrad for a four-week period -- a two-week period, and then followed by -- by my own two weeks' leave, so it puts it sort of middle -- middle of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which period were you in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I was in Tomislavgrad for two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which two weeks?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Towards the middle and end of February, I don't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you took your leave?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Immediately after. And I went to Tomislavgrad so that the doctor who came to cover me in Gornji Vakuf, with Gornji Vakuf being a much more unstable place, had another military doctor for a full four-week period, and I went down to Tomislavgrad to cover the doctor who was based in Tomislavgrad and because there wasn't such an -- wasn't any active fighting in Tomislavgrad it wasn't felt that it needed to have a stable doctor for any period of time particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Talk with a bit slower pace.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Slower, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You referred to these incidents and you mentioned that -- that the person had discharged a -- discharged in a bus a hand grenade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what happened? How did you get involved?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: As I say, we were asked to go and provide additional medical support to our own troops, medical personnel who were on the ground pending the arrival of HVO medical support from Tomislavgrad. On arrival, there was one dead soldier who reported to be the gentleman who had let the pin out of the grenade in his pocket. There were approximately a dozen seriously injured casualties. There were another 20 or so who were reason -- would require medical intervention, specialist medical intervention, and the remainder were minorly injured, cuts and bruises, or not injured at all. Within -- within the detachment there was -- from the HVO side there was -- there was a nurse with them, and she had helped divide the casualties into the -- into the three groups, which is certainly how in the British military -- hence I've given you those figures; the seriously injured, the moderately injured, and the minorly injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And all these HVO soldiers who were in the bus, were they soldiers from Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: A little while after we'd arrived, the commander of -- one of the commanders from Tomislavgrad HVO Brigade came up to the scene, and I had personally to do a double-take because he was either the brother of or the twin brother of the deceased, and I had that moment where I'd looked at the dead body and looked at the gentleman I was just talking to and that was a fairly surreal experience to see the same person, in inverted commas, twice. However, he was quite open with me. We were talking about the poor state of hydration and nutrition of the casualties and how that had made it a little bit more difficult for my junior medical staff to treat the casualties, particularly with getting fluids into them, putting the venflons in, the needles through which the fluids go into the veins, and in casualties who were dehydrated and malnourished that is much more tricky business than you'd normally expect. He went on to explain that, well, of course they were coming back from having just been fighting for the previous 10 to 14 days in Gornji Vakuf and were coming back for a period of R and R, rest and recuperation. He didn't know where -- where I'd previously been working, and he was very -- very open and honest about that and went on to thank us for the medical care that we had delivered to his injured fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been referring in your testimony a couple of times to -- to checkpoints, and I'd like to talk briefly about this again. Did checkpoints already exist in the opstina of Gornji Vakuf at the time you arrived, so in the period prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And during that period of time was it -- and -- well, let me ask you first this: Were there both HVO and ABiH checkpoints in the region?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were checkpoints from both sides when we'd first arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would it have been an equal division of checkpoints as far as ABiH and HVO are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, it appeared that there was fair and even distribution and -- to mark areas of -- of ethnic divide, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in that period did you ever have problems passing through checkpoints in the first few months?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Not at all. Checkpoints from UNPROFOR were seen very much as tip your hat, possibly have a -- a -- a friendly chat, and served in no way to heed our progress around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did that change when the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Very much so. The checkpoints became more numerous. They became more heavily manned and protected. They became more difficult for us to get through, and on some occasions impossible for us to get through, and they occasionally just appeared and disappeared within the space of a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You just said that -- that on some occasions it was impossible for you to get through. Was this -- were those occasions -- were you dealing then with HVO checkpoints or ABiH checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I don't ever recall being held up and impossible to get through a BiH checkpoint. Times I remember the -- the -- it was usually -- when we did have difficulties was when we were doing our aid deliveries, and as I previously said, we were very much delivering 50/50. And I recall going to a -- a Croat village and dropping off our aid and then not being able to progress beyond there up to the BiH village because they -- they didn't need to give us a reason, they just refused to let us pass. And if they're going to leave mines on the road there's not much you can do about it, really, so you can't progress. So that was stopping us from going upwards, and that was usually the time we had difficulties, going upwards. And then coming back we often had certainly a difficult time proceeding back down the hills after we'd done aid drop-offs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever personally threatened at checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: I had one when I personally was threatened and feared for my life, and on a second occasion when I was part of a convoy where we were threatened and as such feared for our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you elaborate? Maybe let's start with the first time you personally were threatened.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We were coming back from having done an aid distribution. The -- we'd dropped of our 50 per cent of aid in the Croat village and had proceeded through that village, but not far beyond there we'd had difficulty getting further up the hill in order to go to a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you remember in which reason -- in which region this was and on what road?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: Yeah. Again, it was -- going from the crossroads, it was going right out of Gornji Vakuf towards Bugojno, and again on the right-hand side of the road. And because of what happened, although I don't remember the name of the village, the drive back I remember vividly and remembered it when I was back in the same area in 1996. So -- so I can be fairly confident that it's -- although I can't remember the name, that's the area in which we're talking, and only about 15 or 20 minutes' drive, if that, from our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We were in my medical armoured vehicle, the 432, and in front and behind us we had two small reconnaissance vehicles, one Scimitar and one Spartan. The -- both of which were crewed by soldiers of the B Company Battle Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who commanded the convoy?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: It was commanded by a gentleman called Captain Nick Short, Nicholas Short, who's 1st Battalion of the Royal Gloucestershire Berkshire and Worcestershire [sic], I think it is - RGBW anyway - Regiment who was a military interpreter. He had deployed with the battle group and been collocated with us in Gornji Vakuf for the duration of the tour, so I'd got to know him quite well, and he'd learnt his local language at the British military language school in Beckinsfield prior to deploying in back end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please continue. What -- what happened?

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: He had shown the HVO checkpoint the back of his vehicle, and they were content. He then showed them the back of our vehicle, my medical vehicle, and there was some light-hearted banter about whether I was hiding any Muslim personnel in the back of my vehicle, and so we lifted up some of the aid that we'd not been able to deliver to show him that we were in fact not hiding any BiH in the vehicle. And they closed the door, and then they went to the rear to inspect the rear vehicle. A little while after that, a minute or two maybe, the door of the ambulance was forcibly opened and an HVO soldier started screaming and shouting and whatever. I do not know what he said, I don't speak that language, but it was clearly not, "Nice to see you and can I come for a cup of tea?" It was something very nasty. And he then cocks his AK-47 and pushes it up against my throat, up here, and into my chin and forced my chin backwards. My RCT driver, a full corporal, sat next to me, the transport driver who was just along for the trip, froze solid. It was one of the few occasions that I've actually seen anybody freeze with fear. Due to a vehicle problem, the intercom between the rear of the vehicle and the commander was broken, and so I was not in a position to be able to talk to the commander. Allowing for how angry, frustrated, and every other kind of emotion this HVO soldier appeared to be exhibiting, I very much feared for my life, and I said in English that I wished he would take the weapon away and that he was hurting me, but nothing happened. And rightly or wrongly, I took the decision that if I didn't do something to alleviate the situation then he would fire the weapon. So I took the decision that I would - excuse to the gentlemen present - but I would kick him where it would hurt in the belief that that would either pull the trigger on the rifle, in which case I'd know nothing about it because I'd be dead and that would be that, or that it would make him stagger and fall over and drop the weapon, which is obviously the consequence it had. Allowing for the fact how long that took and how quickly they'd inspected the rear of the first vehicle and the rear of the second vehicle even with the joke about the Muslims that we were hiding or not hiding in our vehicle, clearly Captain Short had had difficulty getting final clearance for us to move on. We did eventually move on, and on talking to Captain Short when we returned to base, that in fact was the issue, that he had had difficulty negotiating our exit from that checkpoint, and that had put me in the position that I was -- that was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- account. And you were talking about another occasion, and maybe a bit briefer, could you briefly just say what happened on this second occasion.

utterances.speaker: JACQUELINE CARTER
utterances.text: We were coming back again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. To me the story is not complete. At one point you said what your thought was and your conclusion, but you did not tell us whether you did actually act in the way you had planned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did kick him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you're still happy about it, one can see from your face.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if I was happy about it, but it's one of those events in your life that you do not forget rapidly. The second incident was rapidly coming towards dusk one evening, again having done a convoy drop-off.
